objectives: Solve a constructive problem by building the output directly.

screens.question: For which $n$ from 1 to 8 does the pattern fail?

options.text: $n = 1$: one number cannot be an answer
options.why: One number has no neighbours, so no pair differs by 1. `[1]` is a valid answer.

options.text: Every odd $n$
options.why: You looked at the parity of $n$. For $n = 5$, 2 4 1 3 5 has gaps 2, 3 and 2.

options.text: None of them

hints.text: Look only at the joint on each frame.
Frames 2 and 3 have just one even number.
With $n = 2$ or 3 the largest even is 2, which sits beside 1.

feedback.correct: Only $n = 2$ and $n = 3$ fail, at the joint 2, 1.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide through every frame and read the caption.

explain.text: Inside the evens and inside the odds, neighbours differ by 2. The only risk is the joint: the largest even beside 1. That gap is at least 3 once $n \ge 4$.

screens.title: Constructive problems
screens.prose: Problem C is **constructive**: you build an object rather than count one. The method has three parts. Find a pattern, prove it valid, and find the inputs with no answer.
screens.question: Why is evens-then-odds valid for every $n \ge 4$?

options.text: Each block steps by 2, and the joint puts the largest even, at least 4, beside 1
It passed for $n = 4$ to 8, so it passes for every $n$
options.why: You generalised from examples. A proof covers every $n$; eight cases do not.

options.text: An even number and an odd number never differ by 1
options.why: 2 and 1 are even and odd and differ by 1. Parity alone proves nothing.

options.text: The numbers are spread out evenly
options.why: Spread is not the condition. Each neighbouring gap is, and the joint is the one to check.

hints.text: Which neighbouring pairs exist in this pattern?
Pairs inside a block, and one pair at the joint.
Inside a block the gap is 2. At the joint it is the largest even minus 1, at least $4 - 1 = 3$.

feedback.correct: Two kinds of neighbours, and both have gaps of at least 2.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. List the kinds of neighbouring pair and check each.

byKey.examples: You trusted eight examples. A proof checks every kind of neighbour, whatever $n$ is.

explain.text: There are only two kinds of neighbouring pair, so checking both is a proof. An editorial's 'it is easy to see' means exactly this. Writing it down takes a minute and saves a wrong submission.

screens.title: No answer at all
screens.prose: The pattern failed for $n = 3$, but another order might work. In any order of 1, 2 and 3, every number has at least one neighbour.
screens.question: Tap the number that cannot sit beside either of the others.

hints.text: Which numbers differ from 2 by exactly 1?
Both other numbers are within 1 of the middle value.
2 differs by 1 from 1 and from 3, so it has no allowed neighbour.

feedback.correct: 2 has no allowed neighbour, so no order of 1, 2, 3 works.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. For each number, check both possible neighbours.

byKey.c0: 1 may sit beside 3, since their gap is 2.
byKey.c2: 3 may sit beside 1, since their gap is 2.

explain.text: Every number needs a neighbour, and 2 cannot have one, so $n = 3$ prints −1. For $n = 2$ the only two numbers differ by 1 outright. These small cases are the edge cases a constructive problem hides.

screens.title: How the judge marks it
screens.prose: Problem C's checker reads your output and the input $n$. It also knows, from the jury, whether any answer exists. Its verdicts on six outputs for $n = 5$ are listed.
screens.question: Select all that apply: what must the checker test?

options.text: The output has exactly $n$ numbers
Each of 1 to $n$ appears exactly once
No two neighbours differ by 1
−1 appears only when no order exists
The output equals the jury's own answer
options.why: The jury's answer is one of many. 5 3 1 4 2 differs from it and is correct.

options.text: The numbers are in increasing order
options.why: 1 2 3 4 5 is the one order whose every pair fails.

hints.text: Read each 'wrong' verdict: what did it catch?
Lines 4 to 6 each fail a different test.
Length, each number once, the gaps, and −1 only when nothing works.

feedback.correct: Four tests, and none looks at the jury's own order.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A checker tests properties the statement asks for, nothing more.

explain.text: A checker tests exactly the properties the statement asks for. It needs the jury only to know whether an answer exists. The next screen's tests call one.

screens.title: Solve problem C
screens.prose: Write `no_adjacent(n)`. Return a list holding a valid order of 1 to $n$, or `-1` if there is none. A hidden checker, `check_no_adjacent(n, answer)`, marks each test.

lines: Print an order of 1, 2, …, n (1 ≤ n ≤ 10⁵)
in which no two neighbours differ by 1,
If there are several answers, print any.
params.title: Problem C

screens.question: Write `no_adjacent(n)`.

tests.call: all(check_no_adjacent(n, no_adjacent(n)) for n in range(8, 13))

widget.how: Check runs 9 hidden tests. Each calls `check_no_adjacent(n, no_adjacent(n))` and expects `True`. Tests 1 to 7 have $n$ from 1 to 7, and test 8 has 8 to 12. Test 9 has $n = 10^5$, where trying orders one by one cannot finish.

hints.text: Handle $n = 2$ and $n = 3$ first.
`range(2, n + 1, 2)` gives the evens in order.
Return `-1` for 2 and 3. Otherwise return `list(range(2, n + 1, 2)) + list(range(1, n + 1, 2))`.

feedback.correct: Two special cases and one line of construction.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 has $n = 1$. A single number has no neighbours, so `[1]` is valid.
byKey.test-2: Test 2 has $n = 2$: 1 and 2 always touch, so return `-1`.
byKey.test-3: Test 3 has $n = 3$: 2 cannot sit beside 1 or 3, so return `-1`.
byKey.test-9: Test 9 has $n = 10^5$. A search over orders cannot finish; build the evens and the odds directly.

explain.text: Two special cases and one line of construction make an $O(n)$ solution. The checker would accept any other valid order too. At $n = 10^5$ the list is built in milliseconds.

screens.title: Try every order?
screens.prose: A teammate's solution tries orders with `itertools.permutations` until one passes. It is accepted on every test up to $n = 8$. They submit it for $n \le 10^5$.
screens.question: What happens on a test with $n = 10^5$?

options.text: Time limit exceeded: no valid order comes up in time
Accepted: it stops at the first valid order, which comes early
options.why: You assumed an early hit. The orders that begin 1, 2 come first, and every one of them fails.

options.text: Wrong answer: it returns −1 too often
options.why: It is correct whenever it finishes. The problem is how long it takes.

options.text: Memory limit exceeded: it stores every order
options.why: `permutations` yields one order at a time, so memory stays small. Time is the problem.

hints.text: In what order does `permutations` produce the orders?
The first $(n - 2)!$ orders all start 1, 2.
Each order starting 1, 2 fails at once, and $(n - 2)!$ of them come before anything else.

feedback.correct: Correct, but hopeless: $(n - 2)!$ failures come first.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about which orders the search meets first.

byKey.early: You trusted that a valid order comes early. All $(n - 2)!$ orders starting 1, 2 come first, and each fails.

explain.text: A search is a fine brute force for $n \le 8$ and a good stress-test partner for the pattern. For large $n$ only a construction works. A constructive problem with $n$ up to $10^5$ always wants one.

screens.title: The constructive recipe
screens.prose:
You solved problem C in three steps. The same steps fit any 'print any' problem:

```python
# 1. find a pattern on small n (a brute force helps)
# 2. prove it: check every pair, sum or bound it touches
# 3. find the inputs with no answer; print -1 there
```

lines: Print n integers, each from 1 to k,
with sum exactly s, or −1 if impossible.
params.title: Problem F

screens.question: Problem F asks for $n$ integers from 1 to $k$ with sum $s$. When is there no answer?

options.text: When $s < n$ or $s > nk$
When $s$ is not a multiple of $n$
options.why: You looked for equal parts. The numbers may differ: 3, 3, 3, 1 sums to 10 with $n = 4$.

options.text: When $s > k$
options.why: You compared $s$ with one number. Together $n$ numbers can reach $nk$.

options.text: Never: some list always works
options.why: With $n = 4$ and $s = 3$, even four 1s sum to 4, too much.

feedback.correct: The sum can be anything from $n$ to $nk$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the smallest and the largest possible sums.

explain.text: The smallest sum is $n$, all 1s, and the largest is $nk$, all $k$s. Raising one number by 1 reaches every sum in between. So the inputs with no answer are exactly $s < n$ and $s > nk$.

screens.title: Solve problem F
screens.prose: Write `fill_array(n, s, k)`. Start from all 1s, then raise each number as far as it can go until the sum is $s$. Return `-1` when $s < n$ or $s > nk$. A hidden checker marks the list.

state.caption: $n = 4$, $s = 10$, $k = 3$: start at 1, 1, 1, 1 and share out the extra 6.

screens.question: Write `fill_array(n, s, k)`.

widget.how: Check runs 10 hidden tests through `check_fill(n, s, k, answer)`, which expects `True`. Tests 6 to 8 have no answer. Tests 9 and 10 have $n = 2 \cdot 10^5$. Test 9 has $s = 1{,}500{,}000{,}007$, so adding 1 at a time cannot finish.

hints.text: First decide whether an answer exists.
The extra to share out is $s - n$. Each number can take at most $k - 1$ of it.
Give each number `min(k - 1, extra)` and subtract that from `extra`.

feedback.correct: A bounds check, then one pass that shares out the extra.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the first failing test.

byKey.test-4: Test 4 has $k = 1$: every number must be 1.
byKey.test-7: Test 7 has $s = 3 < n = 4$: even four 1s are too many.
byKey.test-9: Test 9 needs about $1.5 \cdot 10^9$ raises if you add 1 at a time. Raise each number by `min(k - 1, extra)` in one step.

explain.text: Each number takes `min(k - 1, extra)` at once, so the loop runs $n$ times. The first numbers end at $k$, at most one sits between, and the rest stay at 1. The checker would accept any other valid list as well.

screens.title: Slicing a parent order
screens.prose: A client order for 1,000 shares must go out as 6 child orders. Each child must be between 100 and 250 shares. The desk needs one valid schedule, and any valid one will do.
screens.question: Select all that apply: which schedules are valid?

options.text: B
C
A
options.why: Two children of 0 shares are below the 100-share minimum.

options.text: D
options.why: The last two children, 50 shares each, are below 100.

options.text: E
options.why: That is 5 children, and the desk asked for 6.

hints.text: Check the count, the sum and each child's size.
This is problem F with sizes from 100 to 250 and $n = 6$.
B and C have 6 children summing to 1,000, each between 100 and 250.

feedback.correct: B and C both pass, so either may be sent.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check count, total and every size for each row.

explain.text: This is problem F with a lower bound of 100, possible exactly when $600 \le s \le 1{,}500$. Interview questions often ask for an example like this rather than a count. Give one valid answer, then say why it is valid.

ideas: A constructive problem asks you to build any valid output, and a checker marks it by its properties.
Find a pattern on small cases, prove each pair or bound it touches, then find the inputs with no answer.
A search over every candidate is a brute force for small $n$, never the solution at $n = 10^5$.
